testName: IISER IAT - Structural Organisation in Plants and Animals (20 Questions) - Version 4

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In a typical dicot root cross-section, the Casparian strips are found in the endodermal cells and are composed of:
options: Lignin and cellulose deposited in the primary cell wall
Suberin and lignin deposited in the radial and transverse walls
Pectin and hemicellulose in all walls of the endodermal cells
Chitin and suberin in the tangential walls only
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Casparian strips are characteristic features of endodermis in roots.
Step 2: They are composed of suberin and lignin deposited in the radial and transverse walls of endodermal cells (forming a band).
Step 3: This creates an impermeable barrier forcing water and dissolved minerals to pass through the selectively permeable plasma membrane of endodermal cells (symplast), preventing apoplastic bypass.
Why others are wrong: (A) Lignin and cellulose are incorrect composition; (C) Pectin and hemicellulose are not Casparian strip materials; (D) Chitin is fungal cell wall component, not plant; tangential walls are wrong location.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the vascular cambium in dicot stems is INCORRECT?
options: It is a secondary meristem that arises from the procambium and interfascicular parenchyma
It produces secondary xylem towards the pith and secondary phloem towards the periphery
It consists of fusiform initials that produce axial elements and ray initials that produce radial elements
It is active throughout the life of the plant and shows no seasonal variation in activity
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Vascular cambium characteristics:
• Secondary meristem arising from procambium (intra-fascicular) and interfascicular parenchyma
• Fusiform initials (elongated) → axial system (vessels, tracheids, fibers)
• Ray initials (isodiametric) → radial system (xylem rays, phloem rays)
• Produces secondary xylem (inward) and secondary phloem (outward)
Step 2: Statement D is INCORRECT - vascular cambium shows seasonal activity in temperate regions, producing spring wood (earlywood) with larger vessels and autumn wood (latewood) with smaller vessels, forming annual rings.
Why others are correct: (A), (B), and (C) are all accurate descriptions of vascular cambium origin, function, and cellular composition.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A student observes the following features in a leaf cross-section: bulliform cells in the upper epidermis, vascular bundles of similar size scattered throughout, and absence of distinct palisade and spongy mesophyll. The leaf belongs to:
options: A typical dicot leaf (dorsiventral)
A typical monocot leaf (isobilateral)
A C4 plant leaf with Kranz anatomy
A succulent xerophytic leaf
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Analyze the features:
• Bulliform cells - large, bubble-shaped cells in upper epidermis characteristic of monocots (e.g., grasses), involved in leaf rolling/unrolling
• Scattered vascular bundles - typical of monocot leaves (like monocot stems)
• No distinct palisade and spongy mesophyll - mesophyll is undifferentiated, isobilateral structure
Step 2: These are diagnostic features of monocot leaf (isobilateral).
Why others are wrong: (A) Dicot leaves have dorsiventral structure with distinct palisade and spongy layers; (C) C4 leaves have Kranz anatomy with bundle sheath cells, not necessarily bulliform cells; (D) Xerophytic leaves have thick cuticle, sunken stomata, not these features.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In the floral formula of family Liliaceae (e.g., Lilium), which of the following correctly represents the perianth, androecium, and gynoecium?
options: K(₅) C₅ A₅ G₍₂₎
P₃₊₃ A₃₊₃ G₍₃₎
K₅ C₅ A₁₀ G₍₁₎
P₍₃₊₃₎ A₍₃₎₊₃ G₃
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Liliaceae characteristics:
• Trimerous symmetry - floral parts in multiples of 3
• Undifferentiated perianth (tepals) - 3 outer + 3 inner, often petaloid
• 6 stamens - in two whorls of 3 (3+3)
• Tricarpellary (3 carpels), syncarpous, superior ovary, axile placentation
Step 2: Floral formula notation:
• P₃₊₃ = Perianth of 6 tepals in two whorls
• A₃₊₃ = 6 stamens in two whorls
• G₍₃₎ = Tricarpellary, syncarpous gynoecium
Why others are wrong: (A) Pentamerous, differentiated calyx/corolla - wrong family; (C) Pentamerous, 10 stamens - not Liliaceae; (D) Incorrect notation and carpel number.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following families is correctly matched with its characteristic fruit type and placentation?
options: Fabaceae - Legume (pod), marginal placentation
Solanaceae - Berry or capsule, parietal placentation
Brassicaceae - Siliqua or silicula, axile placentation
Liliaceae - Capsule or berry, free central placentation
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Analyze each match:
(A) Fabaceae - Fruit: Legume (pod), dehisces along two sutures; Placentation: Marginal (single carpel, ovules along ventral suture) ✓
(B) Solanaceae - Fruit: Berry (tomato) or Capsule (Datura); Placentation: Axile (not parietal) ✗
(C) Brassicaceae - Fruit: Siliqua (long) or Silicula (short); Placentation: Parietal (not axile - false septum divides ovary) ✗
(D) Liliaceae - Fruit: Capsule or Berry; Placentation: Axile (not free central) ✗
Step 2: Only option A is correctly matched.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The process of secondary growth in dicot roots differs from that in dicot stems in that:
options: Dicot roots lack vascular cambium and therefore cannot undergo secondary growth
In dicot roots, the vascular cambium is completely secondary in origin, arising from the conjunctive parenchyma and pericycle
Dicot roots form annual rings but dicot stems do not
The cork cambium in dicot roots arises from the epidermis, while in stems it arises from the cortex
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Secondary growth in dicot roots vs stems:
Dicot Stem:
• Vascular cambium is primary in origin (from procambium) + secondary (interfascicular parenchyma)
• Arranged in ring
Dicot Root:
• Vascular cambium is completely secondary in origin
• Arises from:
- Conjunctive parenchyma (tissue between xylem and phloem bundles)
- Pericycle (especially opposite protoxylem poles)
• Forms a complete ring cutting off secondary vascular tissues
Step 2: Option B correctly describes this difference in cambial origin.
Why others are wrong: (A) Dicot roots DO have vascular cambium and undergo secondary growth; (C) Both form annual rings in temperate regions; (D) Cork cambium in roots arises from pericycle, not epidermis.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In a typical albuminous (endospermic) dicot seed (e.g., castor bean), which statement is CORRECT?
options: The endosperm is completely absent and cotyledons store all food reserves
The endosperm is present as a thick layer surrounding the embryo and serves as the food storage tissue
The perisperm is the primary food storage tissue and endosperm is reduced
The cotyledons are thin and non-functional, with perisperm providing nutrition
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Albuminous (endospermic) seeds:
• Endosperm persists in mature seed as food storage tissue
• Cotyledons are thin (haustorial) - absorb nutrients from endosperm, not storage organs
• Example: Castor bean (Ricinus), cereals, grasses
Step 2: In castor bean, the endosperm is thick, fleshy, and surrounds the embryo. Cotyledons are thin and act as absorbing organs.
Why others are wrong: (A) Describes exalbuminous (non-endospermic) seeds like bean, pea; (C) Perisperm is found in some seeds (black pepper) but not as primary storage in castor; (D) Cotyledons are functional (absorbing), perisperm is not present in castor.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The stomatal apparatus in grasses (monocots) differs from that in typical dicots in that:
options: Grasses have anisocytic stomata with three unequal subsidiary cells, while dicots have paracytic stomata
Grasses have dumbbell-shaped (fusiform) guard cells with two subsidiary cells, while dicots have kidney-shaped guard cells
Grasses lack stomata on the upper epidermis, while dicots have stomata on both surfaces
Grasses have stomata only on the lower epidermis, while dicots have them scattered
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Stomatal types:
Grasses (Monocots):
• Dumbbell-shaped (fusiform) guard cells - narrow in middle, swollen at ends
• Two subsidiary cells (parallel to long axis of guard cells)
• This arrangement allows rapid opening/closing
Dicots:
• Kidney-shaped (reniform) guard cells
• Various subsidiary cell arrangements (anisocytic, paracytic, diacytic, etc.)
Step 2: The shape of guard cells is the key distinguishing feature.
Why others are wrong: (A) Anisocytic is dicot type (Cruciferae), grasses have different arrangement; (C) Grasses often have stomata on both surfaces (isobilateral leaf); (D) Both can have stomata on both surfaces or one surface depending on habitat.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of the family Brassicaceae (Cruciferae) but NOT found in family Fabaceae?
options: Presence of pinnately compound leaves and stipules
Tetradynamous stamens (4 long + 2 short) and silique fruit
Diadelphous stamens and legume fruit
Superior ovary and parietal placentation
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Compare key features:
Brassicaceae (Mustard family):
• Tetradynamous stamens - 6 stamens: 4 long (outer) + 2 short (inner)
• Fruit: Silique (long) or Silicula (short) - dehiscent, two valves with false septum
• Parietal placentation
Fabaceae (Legume family):
• Diadelphous stamens - 10 stamens: 9 fused + 1 free (or sometimes free or monadelphous)
• Fruit: Legume (pod) - single carpel, dehisces along two sutures
• Marginal placentation
Step 2: Tetradynamous stamens and silique fruit are unique to Brassicaceae.
Why others are wrong: (A) Both families can have pinnately compound leaves; (C) This describes Fabaceae, not Brassicaceae; (D) Both have superior ovary; Fabaceae has marginal, not parietal placentation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In the heart of frog (Rana tigrina), the sinus venosus:
options: Receives oxygenated blood from the lungs and delivers it to the left atrium
Receives deoxygenated blood from the body via venae cavae and delivers it to the right atrium
Pumps blood to the systemic circulation through the truncus arteriosus
Is absent in adult frogs and only present in tadpole stage
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Frog heart structure and blood flow:
• Sinus venosus - thin-walled, triangular chamber behind the heart
• Receives deoxygenated blood from:
- Precaval veins (anterior/cardinal veins from head)
- Postcaval vein (posterior from lower body)
- Hepatic veins (from liver)
• Contracts and delivers blood to right atrium
• Left atrium receives oxygenated blood from lungs and skin
Step 2: Sinus venosus is the receiving chamber for systemic venous return.
Why others are wrong: (A) Receives deoxygenated, not oxygenated blood; (C) Conus arteriosus (with truncus) pumps blood out, not sinus venosus; (D) Sinus venosus IS present in adult frogs (reduced/absent in mammals).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The respiratory system of frog shows adaptations for both aquatic and terrestrial life. Which statement is INCORRECT?
options: Tadpoles have internal gills covered by operculum, while adult frogs have lungs, skin, and buccal cavity for respiration
The skin is highly vascularized and moist, serving as a major respiratory organ both in water and on land
Pulmonary respiration through lungs is the most efficient and primary mode of respiration in adult frogs
Buccopharyngeal respiration occurs through the highly vascular lining of the mouth
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Frog respiratory adaptations:
• Tadpoles: Internal gills (covered by operculum), aquatic
• Adults:
- Cutaneous (skin) - major organ, highly vascular, moist, efficient in water and damp conditions
- Buccopharyngeal - lining of mouth and pharynx
- Pulmonary (lungs) - simple sac-like, less efficient than mammalian lungs
• Skin is primary, lungs are supplementary
Step 2: Statement C is INCORRECT - cutaneous respiration is primary, not pulmonary. Lungs are simple and less efficient.
Why others are correct: (A) Correct description of tadpole and adult respiratory organs; (B) Correct description of skin; (D) Correct about buccopharyngeal respiration.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In the male reproductive system of frog, the Bidder's canal:
options: Transports only urine from the kidney to the cloaca
Transports only sperm from the testis to the urinogenital duct
Receives sperm from vasa efferentia and opens into the urinogenital duct
Is present only in female frogs and receives eggs from the ovaries
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Male frog reproductive tract:
• Testes - attached to antero-ventral surface of kidneys
• Vasa efferentia (10-12 tubules) - carry sperm from testes, enter kidney
• Bidder's canal - runs through kidney longitudinally
- Receives sperm from vasa efferentia
- Opens into urinogenital duct
• Urinogenital duct - carries both urine and sperm to cloaca
Step 2: Bidder's canal is the pathway for sperm through the kidney to the urinogenital duct.
Why others are wrong: (A) Urine is transported by collecting tubules and ureter; (B) Sperm go through vasa efferentia first, then Bidder's canal; (D) Bidder's canal is in males; females have oviducts.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The brain of frog is divided into three main regions. Which of the following correctly matches the region with its primary function?
options: Forebrain (prosencephalon) - coordination of muscular movements and balance
Midbrain (mesencephalon) - reception of visual and auditory stimuli, optic lobes prominent
Hindbrain (rhombencephalon) - olfactory interpretation and control of voluntary movements
Cerebellum - production of cerebrospinal fluid and regulation of heartbeat
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Frog brain divisions and functions:
Forebrain (Prosencephalon):
• Olfactory lobes - smell
• Cerebral hemispheres - olfactory interpretation, behavior, voluntary movements
Midbrain (Mesencephalon):
• Optic lobes - large, prominent, receive and process visual stimuli
• Also associated with auditory reflexes
• Major integration center
Hindbrain (Rhombencephalon):
• Cerebellum - coordination of movements, balance (small in frog)
• Medulla oblongata - regulates vital functions (heart, respiration)
Step 2: Option B correctly matches midbrain with visual/auditory reception and optic lobes.
Why others are wrong: (A) Coordination is cerebellum (hindbrain), not forebrain; (C) Olfactory is forebrain, not hindbrain; (D) CSF production is choroid plexus, heartbeat is medulla.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The excretory system of frog includes pronephros, mesonephros, and metanephros stages during development. In the adult frog, the functional kidney is:
options: Pronephros, which is well-developed and functional throughout life
Mesonephros (opisthonephros), which serves as the functional adult kidney
Metanephros, which replaces the earlier kidneys and becomes the permanent kidney
All three kidneys function simultaneously in the adult
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Kidney evolution in frog (amphibian):
• Pronephros - embryonic, anterior, functional in early tadpole, degenerates
• Mesonephros - develops later, posterior to pronephros, becomes functional kidney in adult
• In amphibians and fish, the mesonephros is also called opisthonephros (extends more posteriorly)
• Metanephros - develops in amniotes (reptiles, birds, mammals) as the permanent kidney; does not develop in frogs
Step 2: Adult frog has mesonephric/opisthonephric kidney.
Why others are wrong: (A) Pronephros degenerates early; (C) Metanephros doesn't form in frogs; (D) Only mesonephros functions in adult.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the skeletal system of frog is CORRECT?
options: The vertebral column consists of 9 cervical, 3 thoracic, and 4 caudal vertebrae with free ribs attached
The pectoral girdle consists of scapula, coracoid, clavicle, and procoracoid, but lacks a sternum
The pelvic girdle is fused to the vertebral column via a synsacrum like in birds
The forelimbs have 5 digits while the hindlimbs have 4 digits with webbing
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Frog skeletal features:
Vertebral column: 9 presacral + 1 sacral + urostyle (no free tail, no ribs, no sternum)
Pectoral girdle:
• Scapula - dorsal
• Coracoid - ventral, large
• Procoracoid - anterior to coracoid
• Clavicle - anterior, rod-like
• No sternum (unlike amniotes)
• Glenoid cavity for forelimb articulation
Pelvic girdle: Ilium, ischium, pubis fused to form acetabulum; ilium articulates with sacral vertebra (not synsacrum)
Limbs: Forelimb 4 digits, hindlimb 5 digits (webbed)
Step 2: Option B correctly describes the pectoral girdle components and absence of sternum.
Why others are wrong: (A) No cervical/thoracic distinction, no ribs; (C) Synsacrum is bird feature, frog has simple sacral articulation; (D) Forelimb 4 digits, hindlimb 5 digits (reversed).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In the alimentary canal of frog, the stomach leads to:
options: Directly to the cloaca through the rectum
To the small intestine (duodenum) through the pyloric sphincter
To the large intestine (colon) without any distinct junction
To the liver for initial processing of chyme
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Frog digestive tract sequence:
• Buccal cavity → Pharynx → Oesophagus → Stomach (J-shaped, glandular)
• Stomach → Small intestine (duodenum + ileum) via pyloric sphincter (valve)
• Small intestine → Large intestine (rectum) → Cloaca
• Liver and pancreas are accessory glands with ducts entering duodenum
Step 2: Stomach empties into small intestine (duodenum) through pyloric sphincter.
Why others are wrong: (A) Rectum is after intestine, not direct; (C) There is distinct junction with sphincter; (D) Liver receives blood from intestine, not chyme directly.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The lymphatic system in frog is represented by:
options: Lymph nodes and lymph vessels only, similar to mammals
Lymph vessels, lymph hearts, and lymph spaces (sinuses), but no lymph nodes
Lymph nodes and lymph hearts, but no lymph vessels
Only lymph spaces in the subcutaneous region with no other structures
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Frog lymphatic system:
• Lymph vessels - thin-walled, similar to veins, collect tissue fluid
• Lymph hearts - contractile structures (2 pairs in frog: anterior pair behind transverse processes of 3rd vertebra, posterior pair near urostyle) that pump lymph back to veins
• Lymph spaces/sinuses - subcutaneous lymph sinuses (major spaces), other spaces around organs
• No lymph nodes (unlike mammals) - lymph nodes evolved in amniotes
Step 2: Frog has lymph vessels, lymph hearts, and lymph spaces, but lacks lymph nodes.
Why others are wrong: (A) Frog lacks lymph nodes; (C) Has lymph vessels, lacks lymph nodes; (D) Has more than just subcutaneous spaces.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of the autonomic nervous system of frog?
options: It consists of only sympathetic division with ganglia arranged in a chain
It includes both sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions with distinct ganglia and nerve distributions
It lacks autonomic ganglia and consists only of diffuse nerve plexuses
It is completely absent in frogs, with only somatic nervous system present
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Frog autonomic nervous system:
• Sympathetic division:
- Ganglia arranged in two chains: dorsal sympathetic chain (along dorsal aorta) and lateral sympathetic chain
- Supplies viscera, blood vessels, smooth muscles
• Parasympathetic division:
- Cranial outflow (via oculomotor, facial, glossopharyngeal, vagus)
- Sacral outflow
- More diffuse than sympathetic
• Controls involuntary functions: heart rate, digestion, gland secretion, etc.
Step 2: Both divisions are present with distinct anatomy.
Why others are wrong: (A) Both divisions present, not just sympathetic; (C) Ganglia are present; (D) ANS is definitely present in frogs.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The phenomenon of 'metamorphosis' in frog involves dramatic structural changes. Which hormone primarily triggers and regulates this process?
options: Thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3) produced by the thyroid gland
Insulin produced by the pancreas
Adrenaline produced by the adrenal medulla
Growth hormone produced by the pituitary gland
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Amphibian metamorphosis is regulated by thyroid hormones:
• Thyroxine (T4) and Triiodothyronine (T3)
• Secreted by thyroid gland (two lobes on either side of larynx/trachea)
• Functions:
- Stimulates resorption of tadpole tail
- Promotes development of limbs
- Induces changes in digestive system (herbivore to carnivore)
- Stimulates lung development and gill resorption
- Changes in skin structure
• Prolactin (from pituitary) antagonizes thyroid hormones and maintains larval state
Step 2: Thyroid hormones are the primary trigger and regulators.
Why others are wrong: (B) Insulin regulates glucose metabolism; (C) Adrenaline is stress hormone; (D) Growth hormone promotes general growth but doesn't trigger metamorphosis.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In a comparative study of plant and animal structural organization, which statement is CORRECT?
options: Both plants and animals have specialized conductive tissues (xylem/phloem in plants, blood vessels in animals) that are living throughout their functional life
Plants have indeterminate growth due to meristems, while animals generally have determinate growth and fixed cell numbers in organs
Both plants and animals have an exoskeleton that provides protection and support
Both plants and animals reproduce only sexually through the fusion of gametes produced in specialized organs
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Comparative analysis:
(A) FALSE - Xylem vessels and tracheids are dead at maturity (lignified, protoplast lost); only phloem is living. Blood vessels have living endothelial cells.
(B) TRUE - Plants have indeterminate growth due to persistent meristems (apical, lateral, intercalary). Animals generally have determinate growth - grow to species-specific size, fixed cell numbers in most organs (except some regeneration).
(C) FALSE - Plants don't have exoskeleton; they have cell walls. Some animals have exoskeletons (arthropods).
(D) FALSE - Both can reproduce asexually (plants: vegetative propagation, apomixis; animals: parthenogenesis, budding, regeneration).
Step 2: Only statement B is correct.
